claims.text: Superior ethanol-oxidation performance in nanoscale PtPdRhRuIrOs is governed by isolated noble-metal sites embedded in a disordered alloy matrix.
Atomic isolation in PtPdRhRuIrOs modifies the local d-band structure.
The modified electronic structure optimizes adsorption of ethanol and its oxidation intermediates.
Optimized adsorption promotes complete 12-electron ethanol oxidation.
Atomic isolation reduces poisoning and enhances catalyst durability.
The initial catalyst is a nanoscale, equiatomic PtPdRhRuIrOs solid solution.
Conventional dropwise reduction produces a random distribution with a high degree of atomic isolation in PtPdRhRuIrOs.
Annealing at 200–300 °C under inert atmosphere will promote ordering and partial clustering, reducing site isolation.
The degree of site isolation modulates the local d-band center and adsorption energies.
Isolated Pt, Pd, Rh, Ru, Ir, and Os atoms in the disordered matrix have suitably tuned d-band centers that provide moderate adsorption.
PtPdRhRuIrOs can catalyze ethanol oxidation through a complete 12-electron process.
Annealing-induced loss of site isolation shifts the d-band center and makes intermediate binding either too weak for activation or too strong, causing poisoning.
Loss of site isolation will lower ethanol-oxidation activity and durability.
Relative to the unannealed baseline, the annealed catalyst will have lower ethanol-oxidation current density.
Relative to the unannealed baseline, the annealed catalyst will shift from complete oxidation toward partial products such as acetaldehyde.
Relative to the unannealed baseline, the annealed catalyst will show decreased durability.
The unannealed baseline has high current density, superior complete-oxidation selectivity, and excellent durability.

The proposed mechanism applies in alkaline media at room temperature to highly disordered, compositionally similar nanoparticles below about 5 nm, but may fail with sintering, major compositional changes, or reaction temperatures above 80 °C.
In PtPdCoCuNi, alloying forms isolated Pt and Pd sites, causes charge transfer, strengthens nitrobenzene interaction, and enhances hydrogenation activity.
The quantitative effect of site isolation and d-band shifts in PtPdRhRuIrOs remains unestablished.
